epics.title: Dependency Counterparty Risk Scanner
epics.description:
Working name dependency-scanner. Backlog design, last updated 2026-07-29. A software-composition-analysis tool that crawls a repository's direct and transitive dependencies, constructs the complete known dependency graph, and rates each package and the repository as a whole across security, maintenance, ownership, provenance, licensing and dependency-chain risk.

It is intended to answer more than whether a version has a CVE. It must also answer who the counterparties are that this project depends on; whether a dependency is controlled by one person or a healthy contributor community; whether it is maintained, abandoned, newly created or changing hands; how deep and concentrated the transitive supply chain is; which findings are facts, which are heuristics, and how fresh the evidence is; and what the shortest, highest-impact remediation path is. The scanner produces decision support rather than a claim that a package is safe or malicious, and every score must be explainable from retained evidence.

Goals: discover dependencies from manifests, lockfiles, installed metadata and generated SBOMs; resolve recursively to the deepest graph available from pinned artifacts and trusted package metadata; preserve graph topology, meaning package, version, ecosystem, scope, parent edges, optional, dev and runtime status, and resolution source; enrich graph nodes from reputable, structured, allowlisted sources; calculate facet scores, confidence and an explainable composite rating; detect security, abandonment, maintainer-concentration, provenance, licensing and transitive-chain risks; emit stable machine-readable output plus concise human reports and CI policy results; and remain safe when scanning repositories or package records deliberately crafted to prompt-inject an AI agent.

Non-goals for the first release: proving that source code is non-malicious; executing package installers, build scripts, plugins or repository code; having an LLM browse, interpret or summarize arbitrary dependency content; replacing a legal licensing review or an incident-response investigation; inferring contributor identity across unrelated accounts; and guaranteeing completeness when an ecosystem has no lockfile or authoritative dependency metadata — incompleteness must be reported rather than hidden.
epics.requirements: The threat model and prompt-injection boundary governs the whole design. The scanned repository, package metadata, source repository, maintainer-controlled fields and all network responses are untrusted, because a dependency author can place agent instructions in a README, description, author name, issue, release note, commit message, advisory prose, URL, manifest field or API response. Ten mandatory safety rules. No agent-driven crawling: collection and scoring are deterministic code, and an agent may consume only the scanner's typed output after untrusted strings have been removed or escaped and clearly marked as data. Allowlisted endpoints only: connect only to configured official hosts over HTTPS, never follow a redirect to a different origin, and never fetch an arbitrary URL found in a manifest or an API response. Typed field projection: per source, define a schema and retain only fields needed for a metric — identifiers, versions, timestamps, booleans, numeric counts, enum values, hashes and canonical advisory IDs — discarding descriptions, biographies, README content, commit messages, issue bodies, release notes, HTML and unknown fields. No active repository behaviour: do not install dependencies, import project modules, invoke package managers in script-enabled mode, execute build hooks, evaluate dynamic manifests, or run repository-provided tools. Parser isolation: parse files as data with size, depth, timeout and memory limits, rejecting path traversal, symlink escapes, entity expansion, oversized archives and malformed data safely. Immutable raw evidence: optionally retain raw API responses outside any agent context in a content-addressed audit store, with reports referring to normalized evidence records rather than raw prose. Bounded output: escape control characters, neutralize Markdown and terminal control sequences, and length-limit human-readable package labels. Fail closed on source drift: a schema mismatch or unexpected content type makes that source unavailable, and it must not silently fall back to web browsing. SSRF controls: resolve and connect only to the preconfigured host, reject private, link-local and loopback addresses unless explicitly configured for an internal mirror, and revalidate after DNS resolution. And no secrets in reports: tokens stay in the connector boundary and are redacted from logs, cache keys, errors and evidence. Any future natural-language analysis is a separate opt-in presentation layer receiving the normalized report schema only, with no network or tool access.
epics.acceptance_criteria: The first production-capable release is acceptable when: given supported locked Python or npm repositories, every reachable exact dependency and every path to it appears in the graph or a precise truncation reason is reported; direct, transitive, runtime, development, optional, unresolved, private and VCS dependencies remain distinguishable; vulnerability results combine canonical IDs and ranges, CVSS enrichment and known-exploitation evidence with source and freshness and correct fixed-version handling; reports rate all seven facets with scores, confidence and reason codes; single-contributor and concentrated-counterparty risks are visible with explicit time windows and graph paths; repository and package age, current activity, release cadence, archival state, maintainer turnover and transitive dependencies are represented; missing or stale evidence cannot silently produce a passing enforcement result; prompt-injection fixtures prove arbitrary source prose cannot enter agent context, no arbitrary URL is fetched and no repository or package code runs; JSON, CycloneDX, SARIF and human output agree because they derive from one immutable normalized result; scores are reproducible from the report's policy, formula, connector and evidence versions; offline mode makes no network connection and supports a signed evidence bundle; and the scanner publishes its own pinned dependency inventory and SBOM.
epics.qa_tests:
Eight test categories. Unit, over parsers, purl normalization, range matching, graph algorithms, scoring formulas, policy rules, redaction and canonical serialization. Contract, over recorded official API schemas with unknown and missing field tests, wrong MIME types, redirect attempts, rate limits and schema drift. Graph, over diamond paths, cycles, duplicate versions, optional and platform edges, private, VCS and local nodes, unresolved ranges and truncation. Security, over prompt injections in every string field, terminal escapes, HTML, path traversal, symlink escape, YAML and XML bombs, zip bombs, oversized JSON, malicious registry URLs, DNS rebinding simulation, secret redaction, and proof that no build or install hooks run. Offline, denying all network and proving identical analysis from a pinned evidence bundle. Golden and end-to-end, over small public fixture projects with frozen source responses and byte-stable expected output. Calibration, against a labelled corpus to measure false positives and negatives for the abandonment and anomaly heuristics, with limitations documented. And property and fuzz, over malformed lockfiles, graph invariants, cycles, the range parser, canonicalization and bounded resource use.

Security tests must assert absence: no external prose in normalized reports, no unexpected outbound host, no subprocess, no out-of-root read, and no credential in logs or output.

features.title: Inputs, graph semantics and resolution
features.description: Initial ecosystem support in priority order. P0 Python, from poetry, uv and Pipfile locks, pinned requirements and installed distribution metadata, resolving lockfile first with package metadata only for unresolved edges. P0 JavaScript, from the npm, shrinkwrap, pnpm and yarn locks, taking the exact lock graph without lifecycle scripts. P1 Rust, from the Cargo lock, taking the exact package and checksum graph. P1 Go, from the module files and vendored module metadata, using checksums and proxy metadata without executing project code. P2 JVM, with Gradle or Maven lock and dependency output imported as data, preferring an externally generated SBOM or a locked graph and not running builds by default. P2 .NET, from lock and assets files, taking the exact locked graph. Additional ecosystems are adapters behind one normalized interface, and an adapter must pass parser security tests and graph conformance fixtures before release.
features.requirements:
Dependency resolution rules. Prefer an exact lockfile or an imported CycloneDX or SPDX SBOM over a manifest range. Never pretend a version range is a resolved version. Preserve all paths to a node, deduplicating nodes by Package URL plus resolved version rather than display name. Model cycles safely and impose configurable maximum node and edge limits. Record runtime, development, build, optional, peer, platform and unknown scope. Record whether an edge is declared locally, locked locally, obtained from a registry, or inferred. Include unresolved, private, VCS, local-path, git-SHA and unregistered packages as explicit nodes with reduced confidence rather than dropping them. Detect dependency-confusion candidates: a public package-name collision with a private dependency, an unexpected registry origin, or a namespace change. And report graph coverage — resolved over discovered nodes, unknown edges, unsupported files, maximum depth reached and the truncation reason.

Full graph means all dependencies reachable from authoritative locked metadata and trusted registry records, and the report must state where ecosystem metadata cannot prove completeness.
features.acceptance_criteria: Direct, transitive, runtime, development, optional, unresolved, private and VCS dependencies remain distinguishable, and every path to a node is preserved.
features.qa_tests: The graph tests cover diamond paths, cycles, duplicate versions, optional and platform edges, private, VCS and local nodes, unresolved ranges and truncation. Deduplicating by display name rather than purl plus version is the error that silently merges two different packages.

stories.title: Implement the P0 Python and npm parsers plus CycloneDX import
stories.description: Phase 1's parsing surface. Lockfile first, with package metadata only for unresolved edges on the Python side, and the exact lock graph without lifecycle scripts on the npm side.
stories.requirements: Parsed as data in a resource-limited worker, with no lifecycle scripts run.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Golden fixtures prove exact recursive graphs.
stories.qa_tests: A malicious repository causes no execution and no out-of-root read. A lockfile with a cycle resolves safely. An oversized or malformed lock is rejected rather than crashing.

stories.title: Normalize identity to purl and preserve every path
stories.description: Deduplicate by Package URL plus resolved version rather than display name, and keep all paths to a node.
stories.requirements: Never pretend a version range is a resolved version.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Two packages sharing a display name are distinct nodes.
stories.qa_tests: A diamond produces one node with two paths. Two same-named packages from different namespaces stay separate. A range remains a range rather than being presented as resolved.

stories.title: Keep unresolved, private, VCS and local nodes with reduced confidence
stories.description: Explicit nodes rather than dropped ones, so the graph does not look complete when it is not.
stories.requirements: Reduced confidence, not omission.
stories.acceptance_criteria: An unresolvable dependency is visible in the report.
stories.qa_tests: A local-path, a git-SHA and an unregistered package each appear as nodes with lowered confidence. Dropping them would make an incomplete graph read as a complete one.

stories.title: Detect dependency-confusion candidates
stories.description: A public package-name collision with a private dependency, an unexpected registry origin, or a namespace change.
stories.requirements: Flagged as a candidate rather than a verdict.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A private name that also exists publicly is surfaced.
stories.qa_tests: A private dependency whose name exists on the public registry is flagged. An unexpected registry origin is flagged. A legitimate private-only name is not.

stories.title: Report graph coverage and the truncation reason
stories.description: Resolved over discovered nodes, unknown edges, unsupported files, maximum depth reached, and why truncation happened.
stories.requirements: The report states where ecosystem metadata cannot prove completeness.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A truncated scan says so precisely.
stories.qa_tests: A graph hitting the node limit reports the limit as the truncation reason. A repository with an unsupported manifest reports the file as unsupported rather than ignoring it.

features.title: Reputable source connectors and governance
features.description: Sources are versioned connectors, disabled unless on the deployment allowlist, with official APIs and signed machine-readable feeds preferred over websites. Local lockfiles and SBOMs give the project's actual resolved graph, parsed only and never executed. The OSV API gives vulnerability schema and package or version queries — IDs, affected ranges, aliases, fixed versions and modified timestamps — discarding narrative fields and references. The NVD API gives CVE and CVSS enrichment from API JSON rather than crawled pages. The CISA KEV catalogue gives evidence of known exploitation from official JSON or CSV only, discarding prose. The GitHub Security Advisory API gives ecosystem advisories and patched versions through typed GraphQL fields with no reference URLs. The deps.dev API gives a package graph, versions, projects and advisories as typed fields, where a project link is an identifier rather than a fetch target. OpenSSF Scorecard gives automated repository security-practice signals — check names, numeric scores, reason codes, scan time and commit SHA — from signed release or API JSON, with detail text discarded before any agent output. Official ecosystem registries give package existence, versions, release dates, owners where reliably exposed, distribution hashes and deprecation or yank state, from the exact official host and never following a package-provided URL. The official VCS APIs give repository age and activity, archived state, contributor concentration, releases and ownership changes as IDs, roles, timestamps, counts and enums, without ingesting bios, messages, issue or PR bodies, READMEs or arbitrary repository files. The SPDX license list gives canonical identifiers and deprecation status from signed pinned release data. Sigstore and its transparency log give signature evidence — digest, identity claims, issuer, log index and time, and the verification result — verified cryptographically with no trust in embedded free text. And SLSA gives the provenance vocabulary and verification requirements, scoring only verified attestations rather than self-asserted prose.
features.requirements:
Source precedence for vulnerabilities is canonical advisory identity and range from OSV or the ecosystem advisory, then CVSS enrichment, then known-exploitation evidence. Conflicts are retained as separate evidence with provenance and freshness rather than silently merged. Commercial intelligence may be added later as an optional connector but cannot be required for the open baseline.

Source governance: every connector declares its owner, base URL, schema version, accepted MIME types, field projection, authentication method, rate limits, cache TTL, licence and terms, last compatibility test, and failure behaviour. A connector addition requires a security review and a fixture-based test demonstrating that untrusted prose cannot reach normalized or agent-visible output.
features.acceptance_criteria: A schema mismatch or unexpected content type makes a source unavailable rather than falling back to web browsing, and a partial connector outage produces an incomplete low-confidence result rather than a silent clean bill of health.
features.qa_tests: Contract tests over recorded official API schemas, with unknown and missing field tests, wrong MIME types, redirect attempts, rate limits and schema drift. The redirect test matters most: never follow a redirect to a different origin, and never fetch an arbitrary URL found in a manifest or a response.

stories.title: Implement the four security connectors
stories.description: Phase 2: OSV, NVD, the KEV catalogue and the GitHub advisory API, with version-range evaluation, alias deduplication, fix versions, CVSS, exploitation evidence, conflict handling, caching and source-health reporting.
stories.requirements: Typed field projection on every one, with narrative fields discarded.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Known vulnerable, fixed, withdrawn, conflicting, stale and unavailable-source fixtures all produce the expected explainable result.
stories.qa_tests: Each of those six fixture states. A withdrawn advisory does not count as a live vulnerability. A conflict between two sources is retained as two pieces of evidence rather than merged.

stories.title: Implement the counterparty and provenance connectors
stories.description: Phase 3: official registries, deps.dev, VCS aggregates, OpenSSF Scorecard, the SPDX list, and Sigstore with its transparency log.
stories.requirements: Counts, enums, timestamps and verification results only — no bios, messages, issue bodies or READMEs.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Every score has reason codes and evidence.
stories.qa_tests: A prompt injection placed in a maintainer bio or a repository description does not reach normalized output. A project link is treated as an identifier rather than fetched.

stories.title: Write the connector governance checklist and enforce it on addition
stories.description: Owner, base URL, schema version, accepted MIME types, field projection, authentication, rate limits, cache TTL, licence and terms, last compatibility test, and failure behaviour. A security review and a fixture-based test per addition.
stories.requirements: The fixture test must demonstrate that untrusted prose cannot reach normalized or agent-visible output.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No connector ships without the declaration and the test.
stories.qa_tests: A connector without a declared field projection fails the checklist. A connector whose fixture leaks prose into normalized output fails the test.

stories.title: Fail closed on source drift and report source health
stories.description: A schema mismatch or unexpected content type makes that source unavailable, and it must not silently fall back to web browsing.
stories.requirements: Unavailable, with the outage reported.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A partial outage never produces a silent clean bill of health.
stories.qa_tests: A source returning an unexpected schema is marked unavailable and the report says so. The enforcement result cannot be a pass on evidence that was never collected.

features.title: The seven facets
features.description: Each facet returns a 0-to-100 risk score where 0 is lower observed risk, plus confidence from 0 to 1, an evidence timestamp, source IDs and reason codes. Missing evidence lowers confidence; it does not automatically mean low or high risk.
features.requirements:
A, known vulnerability and exploit risk: vulnerability count by severity and direct or transitive reachability; CVSS base score and vector with version-range matching; known exploitation and ransomware association; exploit maturity when available from an approved structured source; fixed version availability, fix age and upgrade path; and advisory disagreement, withdrawn advisories and evidence freshness. Reachability may modify prioritization only when a supported analyzer can prove it, and not-proven-reachable must never be reported as not-vulnerable.

B, maintenance health: repository archived or read-only state and package deprecation or yank state; age of the latest package release, tagged release and non-bot commit; release cadence over 90, 180 and 365 days relative to the project's own historical cadence, since low churn alone is not abandonment for mature software; time to close recent security and defect reports only if obtained as structured numeric aggregates without ingesting issue content; responsiveness to recent pull requests as numeric aggregates; supported-runtime compatibility and stale dependency usage; and repository and package age, where very new packages receive uncertainty rather than an automatic maliciousness judgment.

C, contributor and ownership concentration: unique non-bot contributors in 90, 365 and 730-day windows; the percentage of commits attributable to the top one and top three contributors; a bus-factor proxy as the minimum contributors accounting for 50 and 80 percent of activity; active maintainers with publish rights where the official registry exposes it; single-maintainer, dormant-owner and maintainer-turnover flags; recent ownership transfer, a sudden new publisher, or a repository-link change; and organization versus personal namespace as evidence rather than a safety guarantee. Bot classification must use explicit account type and a versioned allowlist rather than name guessing alone, and contributor metrics must publish their observation window.

D, provenance and release integrity: locked artifact digest present and matching registry metadata; registry signature, Sigstore verification and transparency-log inclusion; SLSA-compatible provenance attestation and source-to-artifact binding; reproducible-build evidence where a reputable structured source supports it; Scorecard checks such as branch protection, dangerous workflows, pinned dependencies, token permissions, signed releases and vulnerabilities; source repository and registry artifact version or tag correspondence; and mutable VCS references, unpinned URLs and install-time scripts.

E, dependency-chain exposure: direct and total transitive counts; maximum depth, mean depth, fan-in and fan-out, cycles, duplicate versions and ecosystem or registry crossings; the number of distinct maintainers and organizations and the concentration of critical paths under a single counterparty; unresolved nodes and edges, unpinned requirements and private-public ambiguity; native-code, build-time, installer-script, plugin and privileged-runtime exposure flags; vulnerable or high-risk nodes weighted by scope, depth and path multiplicity; and blast radius as the number of root components and paths affected by a node.

F, licence and governance risk: declared SPDX expression, conflicting declarations, and missing or unknown licence; policy classification as allowed, review-required, prohibited or no-policy; copyleft and network-copyleft obligations based on configured organizational policy; and governance indicators — a security policy, a disclosure channel, a release process, a code of conduct — only as booleans from vetted APIs or Scorecard. Licence findings are policy facts rather than legal conclusions.

G, package anomaly and identity risk: typosquatting similarity to existing direct dependencies or popular packages; an unexpected namespace, registry, repository or publisher change; install-script addition, an anomalous version jump, a release burst, or a long-dormant package suddenly republished; package age, extremely low adoption, removed or yanked versions and digest drift. Malware verdicts come only from explicitly approved security feeds, always naming source and timestamp, and heuristics must be labelled anomaly rather than malware.
features.acceptance_criteria: Stable mature projects are not penalized merely for low commit frequency, and single-counterparty paths surface. Score calibration is validated against a curated versioned corpus representing active mature, intentionally stable, abandoned, compromised and new projects.
features.qa_tests: The calibration suite is what keeps the heuristics honest: a labelled corpus measuring false positives and negatives for abandonment and anomaly, with the limitations documented rather than hidden. The two most important negative results are that a mature stable project is not flagged as abandoned, and that a heuristic is never presented as a malware verdict.

stories.title: Implement the vulnerability and exploitation facet
stories.description: Facet A. Counts by severity, CVSS with version-range matching, known exploitation, fix availability and age, and advisory disagreement with freshness.
stories.requirements: Not-proven-reachable must never be reported as not-vulnerable.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Reachability modifies prioritization only when a supported analyzer can prove it.
stories.qa_tests: An unproven-reachability result reads as unknown rather than as safe. A withdrawn advisory is excluded. Two sources disagreeing produce two evidence records.

stories.title: Implement the maintenance health facet
stories.description: Facet B. Archived and deprecated state, release and commit ages, cadence against the project's own history, numeric aggregate responsiveness, runtime compatibility, and age.
stories.requirements: Low churn alone is not abandonment for mature software, and a very new package gets uncertainty rather than a maliciousness judgment. Issue and PR content is never ingested — only numeric aggregates.
stories.acceptance_criteria: An intentionally stable mature project is not flagged as abandoned.
stories.qa_tests: The calibration corpus's intentionally-stable entries score low on abandonment. A genuinely abandoned project scores high. Cadence is judged against the project's own history rather than an absolute.

stories.title: Implement the contributor and ownership concentration facet
stories.description: Facet C. Contributor counts in three windows, top-one and top-three commit share, bus-factor proxy, publish-rights maintainers, and the single-maintainer, dormant-owner and turnover flags plus ownership transfer and repository-link changes.
stories.requirements: Bot classification uses explicit account type and a versioned allowlist rather than name guessing, and every metric publishes its observation window. Organization versus personal namespace is evidence rather than a guarantee.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Single-contributor and concentrated-counterparty risks are visible with explicit time windows and graph paths.
stories.qa_tests: A bot account named like a human is still classified as a bot by account type. A metric without its window is incomplete. A single-maintainer package in an organization namespace is still flagged.

stories.title: Implement the provenance and release integrity facet
stories.description: Facet D. Digest match, signature and transparency-log verification, provenance attestation and source-to-artifact binding, reproducible-build evidence, Scorecard checks, version-tag correspondence, and mutable references, unpinned URLs and install scripts.
stories.requirements: Score only verified attestations, never self-asserted prose.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A verified artifact digest mismatch is critical and stops normal scoring.
stories.qa_tests: A self-asserted provenance claim scores nothing. A cryptographically verified one scores. A digest mismatch halts scoring rather than averaging into a score.

stories.title: Implement the dependency-chain exposure facet
stories.description: Facet E. Counts, depth and fan metrics, cycles and duplicates, maintainer and organization concentration on critical paths, unresolved nodes, exposure flags, weighted high-risk nodes, and blast radius.
stories.requirements: Weighted by scope, depth and path multiplicity.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A critical path concentrated under one counterparty surfaces.
stories.qa_tests: A graph where one maintainer owns every path to a runtime node scores high on concentration. Blast radius counts root components and paths rather than node count.

stories.title: Implement the licence and governance facet
stories.description: Facet F. SPDX expression, conflicts and unknowns, policy classification, copyleft obligations per configured policy, and governance booleans from vetted sources.
stories.requirements: Licence findings are policy facts rather than legal conclusions, and governance indicators are booleans only.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A prohibited licence is a policy failure independent of the security score.
stories.qa_tests: A prohibited licence fails policy with a passing security score. A missing licence reads as unknown rather than as permissive. Governance indicators carry no prose.

stories.title: Implement the package anomaly and identity facet
stories.description: Facet G. Typosquatting similarity, unexpected namespace, registry, repository or publisher changes, install-script additions, anomalous version jumps, release bursts, dormant republication, age, low adoption, yanked versions and digest drift.
stories.requirements: Malware verdicts only from explicitly approved security feeds, always naming source and timestamp. Heuristics are labelled anomaly rather than malware.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No heuristic is ever presented as a malware verdict.
stories.qa_tests: A typosquat candidate is labelled anomaly. A feed-sourced malware verdict names its source and timestamp. The calibration corpus measures the anomaly heuristic's false positives.

features.title: Scoring model and explainability
features.description: Per-package default facet weights, configurable by policy: vulnerability and exploitation 30 percent, maintenance health 15, contributor and ownership concentration 15, provenance and release integrity 15, dependency-chain exposure 15, licence and governance 5, and package anomaly and identity 5. The base score is the confidence-adjusted weighted mean of available facets, with missing facets shown as unknown and weights renormalized only when the policy allows it — and the report always displays coverage and must not compare two scores with materially different evidence coverage without warning.
features.requirements:
Certain facts are policy overrides rather than averages: a confirmed affected version in the known-exploited catalogue is at least critical unless an accepted compensating-control waiver exists; a verified artifact digest mismatch is critical and stops normal scoring; an unresolved package or advisory identity cannot return a pass in enforcement mode; and a prohibited licence is a policy failure independent of the security score. Default bands are 0 to 19 low, 20 to 39 guarded, 40 to 59 elevated, 60 to 79 high, and 80 to 100 critical, with the exact formula, thresholds and reason-code mapping living in a versioned policy file included by hash in every report.

Repository score: do not average all packages, because thousands of low-risk leaves can hide one critical dependency. Repository risk is the maximum of the highest policy-override severity, the weighted 95th-percentile package risk, a critical-path score including runtime and build scope, directness, depth, number of paths and blast radius, and graph-level concentration and coverage penalties. Directness affects remediation priority rather than whether a vulnerability exists, and the report includes both inherent package risk and repository-context risk.

Explainability: every finding contains a stable reason code, the measured value, the threshold, the source, the retrieval time, the evidence age, the affected graph paths, the confidence and the remediation. No score may depend on hidden model judgment.
features.acceptance_criteria: Scores are reproducible from the report's policy, formula, connector and evidence versions.
features.qa_tests: The repository score's maximum-of-four shape is the thing to test against the averaging mistake: a graph of thousands of clean leaves plus one critical node must score critical. The coverage warning is the other: two scores with materially different evidence coverage must not be compared silently.

stories.title: Implement the confidence-adjusted weighted per-package score
stories.description: Seven facets with configurable weights, missing facets shown as unknown, and weights renormalized only when policy allows.
stories.requirements: Coverage always displayed.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Two scores with materially different coverage are not compared without a warning.
stories.qa_tests: A package with three missing facets shows them as unknown rather than scoring them zero. Comparing it to a fully-covered package warns.

stories.title: Implement the four policy overrides
stories.description: Known-exploited affected version at least critical; verified digest mismatch critical and stopping normal scoring; unresolved identity unable to pass in enforcement mode; prohibited licence a policy failure independent of security score.
stories.requirements: Overrides rather than averages.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No override can be averaged away by clean facets elsewhere.
stories.qa_tests: Each override fires on its condition regardless of the weighted mean. A digest mismatch stops scoring rather than contributing a number.

stories.title: Implement the repository score as a maximum of four
stories.description: Highest policy-override severity, weighted 95th-percentile package risk, critical-path score, and graph-level concentration and coverage penalties. Not an average, because thousands of low-risk leaves can hide one critical dependency.
stories.requirements: Both inherent package risk and repository-context risk in the report.
stories.acceptance_criteria: One critical dependency among thousands of clean ones produces a critical repository score.
stories.qa_tests: A graph of a thousand clean leaves plus one critical node scores critical. An averaging implementation would score it low, which is the specific mistake this shape prevents.

stories.title: Attach full explainability to every finding
stories.description: A stable reason code, the measured value, the threshold, the source, the retrieval time, the evidence age, the affected graph paths, the confidence and the remediation.
stories.requirements: No score depends on hidden model judgment.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Every finding is explainable from retained evidence.
stories.qa_tests: Each finding carries all nine fields. The policy file's hash appears in the report, so a score is reproducible from the versions it names.

features.title: CLI, outputs and policy controls
features.description: The command surface: scan a path with a format and a policy, optionally offline and optionally emitting an SBOM; explain a finding against a report; diff two reports; report source status; and validate a policy file. Scan is read-only by default, network enrichment requires explicit source configuration, offline mode uses lockfiles, SBOMs and a pre-populated signed cache, and exit codes distinguish success, policy failure, incomplete scan, invalid input, connector failure and internal error.
features.requirements:
Outputs: a canonical versioned JSON report for automation; a CycloneDX 1.6 SBOM with the dependency graph and vulnerability extensions, with SPDX output possibly following after graph parity tests; SARIF for code-hosting and CI annotations; a text and HTML summary generated strictly from normalized fields; a baseline and diff view covering new, resolved, worsened, improved and evidence-only change; and a remediation list ranked by risk reduction — upgrade, replace, remove, constrain, verify artifact, add waiver, or investigate.

Policy controls: allowed sources, ecosystems, registries, licences and network mode; severity and risk thresholds by runtime, dev and build scope; maximum evidence age, graph size and depth, unresolved percentage and scan time; rules for known-exploited findings, artifact mismatch, unpinned dependencies, unsupported inputs, low-confidence results and source outage; signed expiring waivers tied to a package, version, finding or repository and an owner; and deterministic policy evaluation with no LLM decision point.
features.acceptance_criteria: JSON, CycloneDX, SARIF and human output agree because they derive from one immutable normalized result.
features.qa_tests: Rendering every format from the same immutable result is what makes disagreement impossible, so the test is that a single scan's four outputs report the same findings. The offline integration test proves zero network connections.

stories.title: Build the CLI with distinguishing exit codes
stories.description: scan, explain, diff, sources status and policy validate. Read-only by default, with network enrichment requiring explicit source configuration.
stories.requirements: Exit codes distinguish success, policy failure, incomplete scan, invalid input, connector failure and internal error.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A CI caller can tell a policy failure from an incomplete scan.
stories.qa_tests: Each of the six conditions yields its own exit code. An incomplete scan reported as a success is the failure this prevents.

stories.title: Render all formats from one immutable result
stories.description: Canonical JSON, CycloneDX 1.6 with graph and vulnerability extensions, SARIF, and text or HTML generated strictly from normalized fields.
stories.requirements: One immutable result, so formats cannot disagree.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The four outputs agree.
stories.qa_tests: One scan's four outputs report the same findings and the same scores. Generating any of them from a second pass over the sources would allow them to disagree.

stories.title: Add the baseline diff and the ranked remediation list
stories.description: New, resolved, worsened, improved and evidence-only change; and remediation ranked by risk reduction across upgrade, replace, remove, constrain, verify artifact, add waiver and investigate.
stories.requirements: Evidence-only change distinguished from a real change.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A diff tells a worsened finding from one whose evidence merely refreshed.
stories.qa_tests: A report whose only difference is a retrieval timestamp shows as evidence-only. A newly-fixed finding shows as resolved. The remediation list is ordered by risk reduction rather than by severity alone.

stories.title: Implement deterministic policy evaluation with signed expiring waivers
stories.description: Allowed sources, ecosystems, registries, licences and network mode; thresholds by scope; limits on evidence age, graph size and depth, unresolved percentage and scan time; rules for the named conditions; and waivers tied to a scope and an owner with an expiry and a signature.
stories.requirements: No LLM decision point anywhere in policy evaluation.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Missing or stale evidence cannot silently produce a passing enforcement result.
stories.qa_tests: A scan with evidence past the maximum age fails rather than passing. An expired waiver stops suppressing its finding. A waiver with an invalid signature is refused.

features.title: Data model, architecture and the collect-analyze split
features.description:
The normalized data model's minimum entities: a Scan carrying an id, repository digest, start time, tool version, policy digest, source snapshots, coverage and status; a PackageNode carrying purl, version, ecosystem, namespace, name, qualifiers, directness, scopes, source kind, integrity and an optional repository id; a DependencyEdge carrying from and to purls, the requirement, an optional resolved version, scope, optionality, an evidence id and a resolution state; a Repository carrying provider, opaque id, creation time, archived state, default branch, activity aggregates, contributor aggregates and ownership events; an Evidence record carrying id, source connector, source record id, retrieval time, optional effective time, schema version, normalized fields, optional raw digest and confidence; a FacetResult carrying package purl, facet, risk, confidence, reason codes and evidence ids; a Finding carrying id, rule id, severity, optional package purl, paths, evidence ids, measured value, threshold, remediation and state; and a Waiver carrying its scope, a justification reference, owner, issue and expiry times and a signature.

Free text from external sources is absent from normalized fields. Locally configured waiver justification may be displayed but must be marked user-authored. Reports use stable sorted ordering and canonical serialization for reproducible hashes and diffs.

The implementation is Python 3.12 with typed internal models and no dependency on an agent runtime. The pipeline runs repository or SBOM into safe parsers, then identity normalization, then the graph resolver; allowlisted APIs run through connector projection into an evidence store and cache; and both feed facet analyzers, then policy and scoring, then the renderers. Package boundaries: a CLI surface with exit codes, versioned policy and source configuration, immutable normalized domain models, discovery with file detection and safe parser adapters, ecosystems with purl normalization and graph resolvers, one connector per allowlisted structured source, evidence with cache, provenance and canonical serialization, one deterministic analyzer module per facet, versioned scoring formulas and policy overrides, renderers per format, a security module for URL policy, schema projection, redaction and limits, and test fixtures covering benign, malformed, adversarial and golden reports.
features.requirements:
The processing pipeline, in order: inventory candidate files without following out-of-root symlinks; parse supported lockfiles and SBOMs in a resource-limited worker; normalize identities to purl and construct the local graph and evidence; resolve missing edges only through ecosystem connectors allowed by policy; freeze the graph snapshot, since enrichment must not mutate dependency identity; query sources concurrently with rate limits, retries, circuit breakers and content-addressed caching; validate MIME type and schema, project accepted fields and create evidence; run deterministic facet analyzers and policy overrides; render outputs from the same immutable result so formats cannot disagree; and return coverage, stale or unavailable sources, truncation and the policy result.

Network collection should be separable from analysis: a collect step can create a signed evidence bundle in a networked environment, and an analyze step can operate on that bundle in a restricted environment.
features.acceptance_criteria:
Determinism and auditability: the same graph, evidence snapshot, policy and scanner version produce byte-stable canonical JSON and identical scores; clock-dependent rules receive the scan timestamp explicitly; every external datum is traceable to a connector and a source record id; and formula and connector versions appear in the report.

Reliability and performance: a partial connector outage produces an incomplete or low-confidence result per policy rather than a silent clean bill of health; the cache respects source freshness and advisory modification timestamps; the target for a warm-cache graph of 5,000 nodes is analysis under 60 seconds and peak memory under 1 GiB with network time reported separately; global and per-source concurrency are configurable and official rate limits honoured; and interrupted enrichment resumes without changing the frozen graph snapshot.

Security non-functionals: a least-privilege process with no shell invocation for parsing or resolution; a read-only repository mount where supported; TLS verification, a strict host allowlist, redirect denial, bounded response size, timeouts, decompression limits and per-connector JSON schemas; credentials from a secret provider, scoped read-only and never accepted from scanned files; cache entries and offline bundles carrying source, digest, retrieval time, schema version and an optional signature; and the scanner's own dependency and parser libraries pinned, scanned and kept minimal, with an SBOM published for the scanner itself.

Privacy: do not upload source code, manifests, repository names or complete private graphs to third parties unless policy explicitly permits the exact source; batch queries only by public package identifier and version where possible; and offline mode makes zero network connections, verified by integration test.
features.qa_tests: Byte-stable canonical JSON from the same inputs is the determinism test, and it requires the scan timestamp to be injected rather than read, since a clock-dependent rule otherwise makes every run differ. The offline integration test asserts zero network connections, which is an absence assertion the security category explicitly requires.

stories.title: Define the normalized models and canonical serialization
stories.description: The eight entities, with free text from external sources absent from normalized fields, locally-authored waiver justification marked as such, and stable sorted ordering for reproducible hashes and diffs.
stories.requirements: Immutable, typed, and canonically serializable.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The same inputs produce byte-stable JSON.
stories.qa_tests: Two runs over the same graph, evidence snapshot, policy and version produce byte-identical output. A clock-dependent rule receiving the scan timestamp explicitly is what makes that possible.

stories.title: Freeze the graph snapshot before enrichment
stories.description: Enrichment must not mutate dependency identity, and interrupted enrichment resumes without changing the frozen snapshot.
stories.requirements: Frozen between resolution and enrichment.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A resumed scan analyses the same graph it started on.
stories.qa_tests: An enrichment interrupted and resumed produces the same graph. An enrichment that changed a node's identity would invalidate every evidence link, which is what the freeze prevents.

stories.title: Split collect from analyze with a signed evidence bundle
stories.description: Collect creates a signed bundle in a networked environment; analyze operates on it in a restricted one.
stories.requirements: The bundle carries source, digest, retrieval time, schema version and an optional signature.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Offline analysis from a bundle produces identical results to the online run.
stories.qa_tests: Analysis from a pinned bundle with all network denied produces identical output to the networked run. The offline test asserts zero connections.

stories.title: Implement the security module — URL policy, projection, redaction and limits
stories.description: Host allowlist, redirect denial, SSRF controls with post-DNS revalidation, bounded response size, timeouts, decompression limits, per-connector schemas, field projection, control-character escaping and terminal-sequence neutralization, and secret redaction.
stories.requirements: No shell invocation for parsing or resolution; credentials from a secret provider and never from scanned files.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Prompt-injection fixtures prove arbitrary source prose cannot enter agent context, no arbitrary URL is fetched, and no repository or package code runs.
stories.qa_tests: Prompt injections in every string field, terminal escapes, HTML, path traversal, symlink escape, YAML and XML bombs, zip bombs, oversized JSON, malicious registry URLs and a DNS rebinding simulation. Plus the absence assertions: no external prose in normalized reports, no unexpected outbound host, no subprocess, no out-of-root read, and no credential in logs or output.

stories.title: Meet the performance and concurrency targets
stories.description: A warm-cache graph of 5,000 nodes analysed in under 60 seconds with peak memory under 1 GiB, with network time reported separately, configurable global and per-source concurrency, and official rate limits honoured.
stories.requirements: Network time reported separately, so the analysis figure is a real measurement.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The targets hold on a 5,000-node benchmark.
stories.qa_tests: A benchmark graph of 5,000 nodes meets both figures. Rate limits are honoured rather than retried through, which a contract test against a limiting fixture checks.

stories.title: Publish the scanner's own pinned inventory and SBOM
stories.description: The scanner's dependency and parser libraries pinned, scanned and kept minimal.
stories.requirements: An SBOM for the scanner itself.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The tool can be run against itself.
stories.qa_tests: The published SBOM matches the pinned inventory. Running the scanner on its own repository produces a graph.

features.title: Phased delivery
features.description: Five phases, each with an exit condition.
features.requirements:
Phase 0, decisions and threat-model fixtures: confirm the deployment home, standalone CLI first with a service or API later; define the v1 JSON schema, purl identity rules, policy schema, reason codes and score formula in versioned documents; assemble adversarial fixtures containing prompt injections in every free-text field, malicious symlinks, bombs, malformed locks, cycles and huge graphs; and define the source licensing and terms review plus the connector approval checklist. Exit: schemas validate, threats have tests, and no implementation ambiguity remains about unknown evidence, graph completeness or policy failure.

Phase 1, local graph and safe reports as the MVP: Python and npm lockfile discovery and parsing plus CycloneDX import; purl, scope, path, cycle, unresolved-node and coverage normalization; canonical JSON, CycloneDX and text reports without network access; and graph metrics with policy enforcement for unpinned, unresolved and truncated data. Exit: golden fixtures prove exact recursive graphs and deterministic output, and malicious repositories cause no execution and no out-of-root reads.

Phase 2, security enrichment: the four security connectors; version-range evaluation, aliases and deduplication, fix versions, CVSS, exploitation evidence, conflict handling, caching and source-health reporting; and SARIF plus the report diff. Exit: known vulnerable, fixed, withdrawn, conflicting, stale and unavailable-source fixtures all produce the expected explainable result.

Phase 3, counterparty and provenance analysis: the registry, deps.dev, VCS aggregate, Scorecard, SPDX and Sigstore connectors; the maintenance, contributor concentration, ownership change, provenance, licensing, anomaly and counterparty concentration facets; and score calibration against a curated versioned corpus representing active mature, intentionally stable, abandoned, compromised and new projects. Exit: every score has reason codes and evidence, stable mature projects are not penalized merely for low commit frequency, and single-counterparty paths surface.

Phase 4, ecosystem and operational expansion: Cargo, Go, NuGet and locked or imported JVM graphs; signed offline evidence bundles, CI integrations, waivers, the HTML report and an optional service API; and benchmarking of large monorepos and graph updates plus incremental scans. Exit: the ecosystem conformance suite, performance targets, CI examples, operator runbook and source-governance procedure are complete.
features.acceptance_criteria: Each phase's exit condition is met before the next begins, and the adversarial fixtures from Phase 0 run against every later phase.
features.qa_tests: Phase 0's adversarial fixture set is the asset the whole project leans on, because every later phase's security test runs against it. Building it first rather than retrofitting is what makes the prompt-injection boundary testable at all.

stories.title: Phase 0 — write the versioned schemas and the adversarial fixtures
stories.description: The v1 JSON schema, purl identity rules, policy schema, reason codes and score formula as versioned documents; and fixtures with prompt injections in every free-text field, malicious symlinks, bombs, malformed locks, cycles and huge graphs.
stories.requirements: No implementation ambiguity about unknown evidence, graph completeness or policy failure.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Schemas validate and threats have tests.
stories.qa_tests: Every free-text field in every connector's schema has an injection fixture. This set is what every later phase's security test runs against, so building it first rather than retrofitting is the point.

stories.title: Phase 1 — ship the offline MVP
stories.description: Python and npm parsing plus CycloneDX import, full normalization, canonical JSON, CycloneDX and text reports with no network access, and policy enforcement for unpinned, unresolved and truncated data.
stories.requirements: No network at all in this phase.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Golden fixtures prove exact recursive graphs and deterministic output, and malicious repositories cause no execution and no out-of-root reads.
stories.qa_tests: The golden fixtures are byte-stable. An adversarial repository produces no subprocess and no out-of-root read.

stories.title: Phase 2 — add security enrichment, SARIF and diff
stories.description: The four security connectors with range evaluation, aliases, fix versions, CVSS, exploitation evidence, conflict handling, caching and source health; plus SARIF output and the report diff.
stories.requirements: Conflicts retained as separate evidence rather than merged.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Six fixture states all produce the expected explainable result.
stories.qa_tests: Known vulnerable, fixed, withdrawn, conflicting, stale and unavailable-source fixtures. An unavailable source must not produce a pass.

stories.title: Phase 3 — add counterparty and provenance analysis with calibration
stories.description: Six more connectors, seven facets, and calibration against a curated versioned corpus of active mature, intentionally stable, abandoned, compromised and new projects.
stories.requirements: The corpus is versioned, because the thresholds depend on it.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Stable mature projects are not penalized merely for low commit frequency, and single-counterparty paths surface.
stories.qa_tests: The calibration corpus measures false positives and negatives for abandonment and anomaly, with limitations documented. Thresholds come from corpus results rather than intuition.

stories.title: Phase 4 — expand ecosystems and operational surface
stories.description: Cargo, Go, NuGet and locked or imported JVM graphs; signed offline bundles, CI integrations, waivers, the HTML report and an optional service API; and large-monorepo benchmarking plus incremental scans.
stories.requirements: Each new ecosystem adapter passes the parser security tests and the graph conformance fixtures before release.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The conformance suite, performance targets, CI examples, operator runbook and source-governance procedure are complete.
stories.qa_tests: Per ecosystem: the conformance fixtures and the parser security tests. An adapter shipping without them is how a safe tool acquires an unsafe parser.

features.title: Open implementation decisions
features.description: Five decisions that do not block the specification but must be settled in Phase 0.
features.requirements: Whether v1 ships inside the hive's stateless-tools tree or as an independent package consumed by the hive — independent packaging offers a cleaner trust boundary, and a thin hive-tool wrapper can be added afterwards. Whether GitHub is the only VCS provider in Phase 3 or GitLab ships at parity. Which organizational licence policy becomes the default example, with the engine shipping neutral unless Daniel approves a policy. Whether raw source responses are retained by default, with the recommendation being off by default and content-addressed, encrypted, access-controlled audit storage when on. And calibration thresholds for inactive, maintainer concentration, release anomaly and evidence staleness, which require corpus results rather than intuition.
features.acceptance_criteria: All five settled in Phase 0, because each changes the shape of what gets built.
features.qa_tests: The raw-retention decision is the one with a privacy consequence: retaining raw API responses means retaining untrusted prose, which is exactly what the normalized model exists to keep out, so the storage has to be outside any agent context.

stories.title: Decide the packaging home
stories.description: Inside the hive's stateless-tools tree, or an independent package consumed by the hive. Independent packaging offers a cleaner trust boundary, with a thin wrapper added afterwards.
stories.requirements: A decision, weighing the trust boundary.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Decided before implementation.
stories.qa_tests: Not code. Note the standing preference for stateless tools under their own directory wired via a skill, which argues for the independent package plus a wrapper.

stories.title: Decide whether GitLab ships at parity with GitHub in Phase 3
stories.description: Or whether GitHub is the only VCS provider initially.
stories.requirements: A decision.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The contributor and ownership facets know which providers they cover.
stories.qa_tests: Not code. A facet covering only one provider must say so rather than scoring a GitLab-hosted package as unknown without explanation.

stories.title: Decide the default licence policy
stories.description: The engine ships neutral unless Daniel approves a policy.
stories.requirements: Neutral by default.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No licence policy is assumed.
stories.qa_tests: With no policy configured, a licence finding reads as no-policy rather than as allowed or prohibited.

stories.title: Decide whether raw source responses are retained
stories.description: Recommended off by default, with content-addressed, encrypted, access-controlled audit storage when on.
stories.requirements: If on, the store is outside any agent context.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Retained raw prose can never reach a report or an agent.
stories.qa_tests: With retention on, the raw store holds the response and the report refers to a normalized evidence record rather than the prose. That separation is the whole point of the raw store.

stories.title: Set the calibration thresholds from corpus results
stories.description: For inactive, maintainer concentration, release anomaly and evidence staleness. These require corpus results rather than intuition.
stories.requirements: Derived from the Phase 3 corpus, not guessed.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Each threshold is traceable to a measurement.
stories.qa_tests: Each threshold's false-positive and false-negative rate on the labelled corpus is documented. A threshold set by intuition is the thing this avoids.
